newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine property stocks seen taking a breather.
newsitem.headline: Philippine property stocks seen taking a breather.

text.p: Philippine property stocks may have been battered in recent sessions but brokers said on Monday the sector's boom is far from over.

"Our view is that fundamentals of the sector are firm but it's really sentiment-driven. The sentiment is really bad from the foreign side," Colbert Nocum, an analyst with ING Barings Securities, told Reuters.

The Philippine Stock Exchange's property sub-index, which represents about 25 percent of total market capitalisation, hit a record high 179.38 on July 5, a 50 percent jump from the start of this year.
Since then, it has corrected by almost 15 percent and 69 on Monday fell a further 2.78 points to close at 152.
Analysts are advising investors to buy on dips, or be selective on property stocks.
"Our recommendation is to be selective. We're not bullish on the office sector but on the residential sector," said Barrie del Rosario, an analyst at DBP Daiwa Securities.

ING Barings' Nocum said that, despite expectations of falling domestic interest rates, foreign investors would remain cautious over real estate after being hurt in Thailand and Malaysia, where property prices fell after oversupply in response to strong initial demand in the early 1990s.
Angping Securities was more positive, saying in an advisory to clients: "We would treat further corrections as opportunities for a 'screaming buy' position."
The brokerage does not expect a huge correction in property prices even if the real estate market cools down.
ING Barings estimates the property sector is trading at 24 times forecast 1996 earnings versus the market's 17 to 18 times.
Francisco Licuanan, president of Ayala Land Inc, told Reuters land prices in the premiere financial district of Makati had gone up by 50 percent in the past year and a half.
Real land prices had also more than tripled in residential areas just outside Manila, such in Laguna, Batangas, Rizal and Bulacan, due to the high demand for housing, he said.
Despite the huge jump in real estate prices, Licuanan said he was optimistic for the future, as long as the economy keeps growing.
"As long as the economy is strong, the medium term view is land will go up. All property prices were relatively low. They're only catching up now," Licuanan said.

Expectations of falling domestic interest rates should improve the purchasing power of the middle-income group, DBP-Daiwa Securities said in a study, with a projected shortfall of over 1.2 million housing units by the end of 1998.
In the office sector, it said there could be oversupply from 1998 even if demand remains strong with the recovery of the Philippine economy.
